background.definition: Wrist fractures encompass fractures of the distal radius, distal ulna, and carpal bones. Distal radial fracture is a fracture of the distal radial metaphysis. A distal radius fracture may also be accompanied by a fracture of the ulna and/or carpal bones. The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Scaphoid fractures can involve the distal pole, the waist, or the proximal pole. In adults, the majority of scaphoid fractures occur in the waist of the scaphoid.

list.listitem: Distal radial fractures: bimodal age distribution, with peaks occurring in children and in the elderly.
The incidence of distal radius fractures in persons 35 years of age and over is 36.8 per 10,000 per year in women and 9.0 per 10,000 per year in men.
The incidence of acute scaphoid fractures is 7.3 per 10,000 per year in men, and 1.5 per 10,000 per year in women; the highest incidence is in men between the ages of 20 and 30 years.
Patients with a high functional requirement may experience a significant loss of function, if proper bone healing and alignment are not achieved.
Fall on an outstretched hand
Direct trauma
The wrist is a highly mobile structure, composed of the radius and a large number of smaller bones and joints working in unison to provide its global range of motion.

Factors affecting wrist fractures are: (1) direction of three-dimensional loading; (2) magnitude and duration of force; (3) position of the hand and wrist at the time of injury; and (4) biomechanical properties of ligaments and bones.
Athletes represent a special population. Their wrist injuries can occur either from a single acute event or as part of a continuum of overuse that leads to osseous failure.

The proximal pole of the scaphoid is supplied by dorsal vessels, which enter the waist of the scaphoid and travel in a retrograde, distal-to-proximal fashion. Therefore, fractures of the proximal pole take a longer time to heal and have a higher risk of nonunion and avascular necrosis.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Decreased bone density at distal radius
History of previous fracture after the age of 50 years

Multidisciplinary interventions targeting multiple risk factors are effective in reducing the incidence of falls.B

list.listitem: Fractures of the distal radius can be classified according to the mechanism of injury. Type 1: bending fractures; type 2: shearing fractures; type 3: compression fractures; type 4: avulsion fractures; type 5: combined fractures.

Fractures of the scaphoid can be classified as follows. Type A: stable and include fractures through the tubercle of the scaphoid and undisplaced fractures through the waist of the scaphoid; type B: unstable and include oblique fractures through the distal pole of the scaphoid, displaced or mobile fractures of the waist of the scaphoid, proximal pole fractures, fracture dislocations, and comminuted fractures; type C: delayed union; type D: established nonunion.

Obtain a thorough history. Identify the mechanism of injury. Inspect for swelling, deformity, open fractures, and other injuriesm palpate to identify any deformities and areas of tenderness, and assess wrist range of motion.

Examine areas distal and proximal to the injured area to identify any other concomitant injuries. Assess neurovascular status in the hand before and after any manipulation or reduction attempts. History and usual mechanism for specific fractures are discussed below.

Adults with injured wrists who have no deformity, no edema, no pain with pronation are unlikely to have fractures. This externally validated test is 98.7% sensitive with a negative likelihood ratio of 0.04 (false negative rate 1.3%). Using this decision rule could reduce use of xrays by 16%.

Distal radial fractures: on history, fall on an outstretched hand with resulting wrist pain; on PE, wrist swelling, ecchymosis, tenderness over distal radius. When scaphoid fracture is clinically suspected, it is diagnosed between 12% and 57% of the time.

Scaphoid fractures: radial wrist pain after fall on an outstretched hand while skating, skateboarding, bicycling, or participating in contact sports; on examination, usually no swelling or ecchymosis, with only slight decrease in wrist range of motion; examine for tenderness of the scaphoid in the "anatomic snuff box" (90% sensitive, 40% specific, LR+ 1.5, LR− 0.25), tenderness of the scaphoid tubercle (87% sensitive, 57% specific, LR+ 2.0, LR− 0.2), and scaphoid compression tenderness elicited by applying axial pressure to the scaphoid via the first metacarpal. A systematic review found that absence of snuffbox tenderness makes scaphoid fracture considerably less likely (LR− 0.15).

Hook of the hamate fractures: racquet or club sports, with forceful swing causing racquet or club to impact on hook of hamate, resulting in ulnar-sided wrist pain; on examination, pain to palpation of hypothenar area, as well as on resisted flexion of fourth and fifth fingers.

Body of the hamate fractures: usually axial load injury to clenched fist, with associated fracture dislocations of fourth and fifth carpometacarpal (CMC) joints and fractures of fourth and fifth metacarpal bases; on examination, pain with axial load and characteristic deformity resulting from metacarpal fractures.

Triquetral fractures: usually wrist forced to extreme flexion, or wrist forced into dorsiflexion and ulnar deviation, with ulnar-sided pain; on examination, ulnar-sided ecchymosis, tenderness, may have larger ulnar styloid, which predisposes to this injury.
Pisiform fractures: ulnar-sided wrist pain after fall on outstretched hand; on PE, tenderness over pisiform.

Capitate fractures: wrist pain after direct blow on wrist, fall with wrist in dorsiflexion and ulnar deviation (with dorsal radius impacting on waist of the capitate), or associated with a perilunate dislocation; on examination, swelling, ecchymosis, and tenderness over capitate.

Lunate fractures: rare; on history, may be due to loading of wrist in hyperextension with one direct injury or with multiple, repetitive trauma, with pain over dorsum of wrist centrally; on examination, tenderness over central dorsum of wrist, swelling, decreased wrist motion, weakness, and diminished grip strength.

Trapezial ridge fractures: on history, may be due to a direct blow or an avulsion injury with associated trapezial ridge fractures or hook of the hamate fractures, with pain over the thenar area; on PE, painful and weak pinch, tenderness to direct palpation, pain with resisted flexion while wrist is held in dorsiflexion.

Trapezial body fractures: uncommon; on history, usually a result of axial loading or shearing mechanism across first CMC joint; may be associated with fractures of first metacarpal base or the scaphoid; on PE, painful and weak pinch, tenderness to direct palpation, pain with resisted flexion while wrist is held in dorsiflexion.

Trapezoid fractures: least common fractures; usually dislocated, not fractured; on history, fracture usually is due to an axial loading of the index metacarpal; on PE, direct tenderness on PE, painful and weak pinch, tenderness to direct palpation, pain with resisted flexion while wrist is held in dorsiflexion.

In a patient with wrist trauma, initial imaging should consist of PA, lateral, and semipronated oblique radiographs of the wrist. In addition to the above views, an elongated PA view with approximately 30° of cephalad beam angulation and the wrist positioned in 10° to 15° of ulnar deviation is recommended as a routine when there is a clinical suspicion for a scaphoid fracture. Key measurements on radiographs of the wrist: (1) radial inclination (), (2) radial height (), and (3) radial tilt ().

Point of care ultrasound (POCUS) is also highly accurate and is an excellent alternative to radiographs in adults and children. in a study of 270 children with non-deformed suspected distal forearm fracture, POCUS was 98% sensitive and 100% specific compared to expert panel reviewing all imaging, and was more accurate overall than radiographs.

Assess radiographs for: (1) distal radioulnar joint involvement, (2) radiocarpal joint involvement, and (3) stability. Factors that contribute to instability: (1) dorsal comminution >50% of the width laterally, (2) palmar metaphyseal comminution, (3) dorsal tilt >20°, (4) initial displacement >1 cm, (5) initial radial shortening >5 mm, (6) intraarticular disruption, (7) associated ulnar fracture, and (8) severe osteoporosis and age >60 years.

In a patient with a suspected distal radial fracture and negative initial radiographs, the wrist may be casted, with repeat radiographs in 10 to 14 days, or a CT or MRI of the wrist may be obtained to confirm or exclude a fracture immediately. A systematic review concluded that MRI is superior to CT, bone scan or ultrasound, with the added benefit of identifying other causes of the injury.

In a patient with a suspected scaphoid fracture and negative initial radiographs, the wrist should be placed in a thumb spica cast, with repeat radiographs in 10 to 14 days, or a CT or MRI of the wrist may be obtained to confirm or exclude a fracture immediately. A cost effectiveness analysis confirmed that CT or MRI is cost-effective following negative radiograph in patients with injury suspicious for scaphoid fracture. If there is concern for displacement in a patient with a confirmed scaphoid fracture, obtain a MRI or CT scan of the wrist. Bone scintigraphy is sensitive but less specific than CT or MRI for scaphoid fracture, and ultrasound is less sensitive.

In patients with wrist injuries, a systematic review concluded that neither clinical exam nor MRI had significant negative predictive value to rule out ligament injuries. When imaging is normal but clinical suspicion remains high for ligament injury, wrist arthroscopy is recommended.

Point of care ultrasound (POCUS) is increasingly used to evaluate fractures. One study found that compared with radiography, it was 98% sensitive and 96% specific for detecting distal radius fractures.
In children 5-15 years old POCUS is highly senstive (97.9%) and specific (100%) to diagnose distal forearm fractures.
Diagnostic testing for specific fractures is described below:

Comminuted distal radial fracture and suspected joint incongruity: in this situation, also obtain a CT scan of the wrist. In a patient with a suspected distal radioulnar joint subluxation, obtain a CT scan of the wrists in both a prone and a supinated position.
Hook or body of the hamate fracture: If suspected, CT scan may be helpful for preoperative planning.

Triquetral fracture: If suspicion for triquetral fracture remains high and diagnosis is not clear with standard radiographs, inspect oblique radiographs more carefully, obtain a radiograph with the hand in slight pronation (which brings the triquetrum into profile), or obtain a CT scan.

Pisiform fractures: A lateral radiograph with the wrist in slight supination will profile the pisiform. A carpal tunnel view may be helpful as well. If radiographs are inconclusive and suspicion remains high, obtain a CT scan.
Capitate fractures: If initial radiographs are negative but suspicion is high, immobilize and do close followup radiographs; if with persistent pain, an MRI should be considered.
Lunate fractures: Plain x-rays are often inconclusive; if with high index of suspicion, consider an MRI.
Trapezium fractures: These may be missed on standard radiographs; carpal tunnel view should highlight the trapezial ridge. If radiographs are inconclusive, obtain a CT scan.
Trapezoid fractures: Consider CT scan if suspicion is high and radiographs are inconclusive.

Scapholunate ligament tear: For patients with a tear of the scapholunate ligament, the posteriod radioscaphoid angle was 80% sensitive and 90% specific for scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC) wrist.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation and management.

In a patient with a suspected distal radial fracture or scaphoid fracture and negative initial radiographs, the wrist may be casted, with repeat radiographs in 10 to 14 days, or an MRI of the wrist may be obtained to confirm or exclude a fracture immediately.C
For patients with nondisplaced or minimally displaced (<= 2 mm) scaphoid fracture, non-surgical management results in a higher rate of non-union (8% vs 1%) but fewer complications (2.6% vs 9%).B
Volar plating should be considered for intraarticular fracture, external fixation for extra-articular fracture, and cast immobilization for older patients.A
AAOS guidelines provide an overview of evidence-based treatment recommendations for patients with distal wrist fracture.

A network meta-analysis of 70 RCTs with 4789 patients concluded that there was no clinically important difference between surgical approaches at one year. Volar plating had fewer complications for patients with intraarticular fracture, and external fixation had fewer complications in those with extraarticular fractures. Non-operative treatment should be strongly considered for older patients.
Follow-up radiography at 6 and 12 weeks did not improve outcomes at one year in a randomized trial of 326 patients with distal radial fracture.

Surgical options for distal radius fractures: percutaneous pinning, external skeletal fixation, open reduction and internal fixation, and arthroscopically assisted reduction. A Cochrane review, now withdrawn though, concluded that not enough evidence exists to tell when surgery gives a better result, nor which type of surgery is the best. Evidence is also lacking regarding when moderately displaced distal radial fractures should be manipulated back into position, duration of immobilization, or which method of closed reduction is best.

The use of external fixation for dorsally displaced fractures of the distal radius in adults has some evidence. Although there is insufficient evidence to confirm a better functional outcome, external fixation reduces redisplacement, gives improved anatomical results, and most of the excess surgically related complications are minor.

A more recent meta-analysis concluded that internal fixation was superior to external fixation for the treatment of distal radial fracture, with lower rates of disability, better rehabilitation, and lower infection rates.

A randomized controlled trial of 140 patients with distal radial fracture found that volar locking plate (VLP) fixation was better than plaster splint in terms of function based on DASH and PRWE score. Complication rates were similar.

A slightly larger RCT compared VLP with exterial fixation in 156 patients and found that while the VLP group had faster recovery of function and less pain, at one year there was no functional difference and no difference in complications.

An RCT randomized 92 patients with displaced extra-articular radial fracture to operative vs. non-operative treatment. Those assigned to open reduction and volar plate fixation had better functional outcomes, and 18 of 44 non-operative patients underwent subsequent surgery.

A study randomized 100 adults 65 years and older with displaced distal radial fracture (>10 degrees dorsal angulation, ulnar variance >3 mm or intra-articular step-off >2 mm) to cast immobilization or surgery with VLP. Although there was no significant difference in outcomes at one year, patients managed operatively had a faster recovery and were more satisfied with their care.

A trial randomized 166 adults with distal radial fracture to open reduction and internal fixation using a volar-locking plate (ORIF/VLP) or closed reduction and cast immobilization. At 3, 12 and 24 months there were no differences other than patient reported treatment success, which was greater with ORIF/VLP (75% vs 45%, NNT = 3, p = 0.002).

AAOS guidelines found moderate evidence to support operative (as opposed to cast fixation) for any distal radial fracture with post-reduction radial shortening greater than 3 mm, dorsal tilt greater than 10°, or intra-articular displacement of step-off greater than 2 mm.

Pain control during reduction of a distal radius fracture can be achieved using a hematoma block, conscious sedation, interscalene block, or general anesthesia. There is no good RCT evidence to decide between these method of anesthesia when treating a fractured wrist. A Cochrane review concluded that multiple injections are preferable to single or double injection techniques for axillary brachial plexus block in adults.

Clinical outcomes are similar for general versus regional anesthesia in patients with distal radial fracture. Opioid consumption was higher in the first 24 hour in the general anesthesia group but higher in the regional anesthesia group after discharge.
An RCT with 116 adults with non-operatively treated distal radius fracture found no advantage of face-to-face rehabilitation over simply offering an advice leaflet or advice video.

In an RCT of 149 patients with a distal radius buckle fracture who were splinted, there was no difference in outcomes whether they removed the splint after 1 to 2 weeks and saw a physician as needed only, or saw their primary care physician in 1 to 2 weeks.
Scaphoid fractures
Percutaneous screw fixation, internal fixation, and in some cases bone graft are surgical options.

However, not all scaphoid fractures require surgery. In 2020, a study randomized 439 participants with bicortical fracture of the scaphoid waist (≤2 mm displacement) to immediate surgical fixation or cast immobilization followed by immediate fixation if non-union of fracture occurred. At one year there was no difference between groups in patient-related wrist evaluation scores or other outcomes, other than more complications in surgery.

A systematic review identified 7 studies of adults with nondisplaced or minimally displaced (< 2 mm) scaphoid fracture; 98% were at the waist of the scaphoid. Functional outcomes are similar at one year for surgical and non surgical treatment for minimally displaced scaphoid fractures. There was a tradeoff between more non-union (8% vs 1%) but fewer complications (2.6% vs 9%) with non-surgical management.
After 5 years, outcomes are similar for cast immobilization and surgery for minimally displaced scaphoid fractures.

Scrub the dorsum of the distal forearm with betadine over fracture site. Insert a sterile needle in to the area of bony deformity. Aspirate the syringe. A flashback of blood in the syringe indicates that the needle tip is in the hematoma. Inject 5 to 10 mL of 2% Lidocaine (without epinephrine) directly into the hematoma.
Insufficient evidence regarding effect of hyperbaric oxygen treatment for the management of bony fractures that had delayed union or established nonunion.
Vitamin C, 500 mg PO daily for 50 days, after a wrist fracture prevents reflex sympathetic dystrophy.
Postreduction, begin early active range of motion exercises for the shoulder, elbow, and fingers.

An RCT with 81 patients with distal radial fracture found that an accelerated rehab protocol helped patients return to their previous level of function more quickly than a standard protocol. However, a Cochrane review concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine the best form of rehabilitation for patients with distal wrist fractures.
However, a pragmatic RCT in patients 60 and older with distal radius fracture found no difference between those randomized to supervised physical therapy or home exercises.
A trial randomized 52 adults 60 years and older to a home hand strengthening exercise program or finger movement (sham). At 6 and 12 weeks, grip strength was better in the intervention group.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation and conservative management, and for management of specific fracture types.
Always begin immobilization with a splint; switch to a cast once soft tissue swelling subsides.
Signs of adequate closed reduction of a distal radius fracture: radial shortening <5 mm, radial inclination ≥15°, dorsal radial tilt <15°, volar radial tilt <20°, articular incongruity ≤2 mm.

Patients with an acute nondisplaced fracture of the scaphoid waist can be managed conservatively by immobilization in a short-arm thumb spica cast or surgically with screw fixation. Patients treated with either modality show no significant differences in range of motion of the wrist or grip strength; however, surgically managed patients show significantly faster bony union and earlier return to work.

A randomized trial in 865 children with torus fractures of the distal radius, soft bandages and rigid immobilization (with either a splint or a cast) are comparable with regard to pain, function, and quality of life.
A network meta-analysis of 13 RCTs with 3898 participants found no evidence to support the routine use of prophylactic antibiotics for patients undergoing surgery for hand trauma.

Duration of immobilization for a conservatively managed distal radial fracture has generally been recommended to be 5 to 6 weeks. However, a trial randomized 150 patients aged 65 and older with displaced distal radial fracture who were being managed conservatively to 4 versus 6 weeks of immobilization. There was no difference in pain, function, and complications between groups.

Duration of immobilization for a conservatively managed scaphoid fracture: 6 to 12 weeks. The duration of immobilization depends on the location of the fracture; as the fracture line moves proximally, the required duration of immobilization also increases.
Immediate referral is indicated for patients with open fractures, severe compression neuropathies, and vascular impairment.

Patients with unstable fractures, volarly displaced distal radius fracture, intraarticular distal radius fracture with dislocation of the radiocarpal joint, fracture of the radial styloid, and associated carpal bone fractures should be referred.

Refer patients with associated compartment syndrome, articular step off >2 mm, bilateral distal radius fractures, other concomitant fractures of the involved extremity, failed conservative management, high functional requirement, displaced fractures of the scaphoid, and proximal pole fractures of the scaphoid.
Isolated distal ulnar fractures are exceedingly rare and for this reason should be referred to an orthopedic surgeon.
For patients with distal radius fractures, restoration of normal anatomy is important for the restoration of function.C
Prognosis of scaphoid fractures depends on the location of the fracture and the presence or absence of displacement.C
The reported incidence of nonunion with delayed immobilization of scaphoid fractures ranges from 19% to 88%.
The majority of patients with an untreated scaphoid nonunion fracture will go on to develop osteoarthritis of the involved wrist.

For patients with distal radius fractures, restoration of normal anatomy is important for the restoration of function. Grip strength, range of motion, and ability to perform activities of daily living are significantly worse in patient's with malunited versus anatomically healed distal radial fractures.C

Complications of distal radius fractures: nerve injury, open injury, compartment syndrome, loss of reduction, infection, complex regional pain syndromes, posttraumatic arthrosis, nonunion/delayed union, malunion.

Prognosis of scaphoid fractures depends on the location of the fracture and the presence or absence of displacement; fractures involving the proximal pole and displaced fractures are at a higher risk for nonunion and avascular necrosis.C
For patients with a tear of the scapholunate ligament, the posteriod radioscaphoid angle was 80% sensitive and 90% specific for scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC) wrist.
Always assess neurovascular status in the hand before and after any manipulation or reduction attempts.

For distal radius fractures managed conservatively, obtain radiographs at the end of the first and second weeks to detect redisplacement. There appears to be no benefit to subsequent radiographs unless clinically indicated. A trial randomized 326 patients with distal radial fracture to routine radiographs at 6 and 12 weeks or no radiographs, and found no differences in any outcomes at one year.
For fractures of the scaphoid being managed conservatively: obtain CT at the end of 6 weeks; in case of incomplete healing, continue immobilization for another 6 weeks.
For the first few days after casting, keep the affected extremity elevated above the level of the heart to reduce swelling.
Once the affected extremity has been casted, perform active movements in the fingers of that hand.
Seek immediate medical care if patient develops any symptoms of compartment syndrome (severe pain, neurologic changes, discoloration in the affected extremity).
Keep the cast clean and dry, and examine it daily for cracks and weak spots.
Most distal radial fractures in older low-demand patients can be treated conservatively with a satisfactory functional outcome.

feature.caption: Treatment of Wrist Fractures in Adults.
feature.feature_body:
Fracture Treatment
Distal radius fractures
Use a short arm cast after placing the wrist in a plaster or sugar tong splint for 7-10 days. Elevate for 4-7 days to prevent or reduce swelling, with the hand higher than the heart. Tight cast problems may be prevented by giving the patient instructions on watching out for numbness, tingling, pain, swelling, or decreased sensation in the wrist or hand. Up to 2 weeks of analgesics and/or nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs may be needed. Recheck the fracture at 7 days, then at 2-week intervals, until it is healed. To ensure that the fracture has not slipped, repeat x-rays at 7 days and at 2 weeks. At 5 weeks, get x-rays again; the cast may be removed at that time in most cases. At each visit, estimate a return-to-work date for temporary transitional and for regular work, and prescribe temporary transitional and job modifications.
Scaphoid fractures
If clinical suspicion of a scaphoid fracture is high because of localized pain at the snuff box following fall or trauma, but x-rays are negative, a short arm thumb spica cast should be used for 7-10 days. Then, to clarify the diagnosis, a repeat x-ray with the wrist out of plaster is obtained. Rarely, to confirm a suspected diagnosis of scaphoid fracture, a bone scan may be useful. Confirmed scaphoid fractures should be immobilized in a short arm thumb spica cast for 10-12 weeks until healed by x-ray examination. Analgesics and/or NSAIDs may be appropriate for up to 2 weeks. Recheck the wrist at 7 days and then at 2-week intervals until the fracture is healed; treatment may take as long as 12-36 weeks. At 4-6 weeks, wrist x-rays should be taken. To obtain the quality of x-rays necessary to determine healing status, it is often necessary to remove the cast. Delayed union manifests as a persistent fracture line on x-ray with continued tenderness over the scaphoid. The patient should be referred for surgery if delayed union is suspected. At each visit, estimate a return-to-work date for temporary transitional and regular work, and prescribe temporary transitional and job modifications, including a brace to prevent reinjury.
Hook of the hamate fractures
If displacement is minimal, and the patient is being seen within 7 days postinjury, cast immobilization can provide good healing. Patients with significantly displaced fractures should be referred to a hand surgeon for possible fixation with or without bone grafting or hook excision.
Body of the hamate fractures Usually associated with displacement or subluxation of the fourth and fifth CMC joints, so referral for open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) is recommended, especially because of the motion that occurs in these joints.
Triquetral fractures
If isolated "chip" fracture, rigid immobilization in a cast for 4-6 weeks, followed by graded rehabilitation program usually leads to good long-term functional outcomes. For the uncommon triquestral body fractures, there is not enough good data to give definitive treatment guidelines. Fractures with perilunate dissociation or with more than 1-mm displacement should be referred for possible surgery to maximize long-term wrist function.
Pisiform fractures
Initial treatment is 4-6 weeks of cast immobilization followed by a graded therapy program. Pisiform excision offers reliable pain relief for patients who have persistent problems.
Capitate fractures
Rare injury; for undisplaced fractures, cast immobilization is sufficient. For displaced fractures, a variable-pitch headless screw or K-wire may be used to do ORIF through a dorsal approach.
Lunate fractures
Four to six weeks of cast immobilization is appropriate for minimally displaced fractures. ORIF is justified for displaced fractures of the lunate body.
Trapezium fractures
Cast immobilization should be attempted for trapezial ridge fractures. Referral for possible surgical excision should be made for ongoing symptoms of trapezial ridge fractures. Trapezial body fractures commonly involve the first CMC joint, which is placed under great stress with pinching, so an anatomic reduction of the joint surface is recommended for these fractures.
Trapezoid fractures
Least commonly fractured carpal bone; usually dislocated, not fractured; closed reduction is recommended for dislocations. ORIF is warranted to restore the carpal arch of the hand, if closed reduction fails or fracture fragments remain displaced.
